readme: To add an event, see README.md in this folder. The page sorts this list by date, so order here does not matter. dateNote, imageNote, note, and sources[].note are the hover and tap tooltips. image is the thumbnail; imageFull opens when the thumbnail is clicked.

events.dateNote: YouTube lists the publish date as 17 September 2019, on OpenAI’s channel.
events.title: OpenAI shows multi-agent hide and seek
events.summary: On 17 September 2019 OpenAI posted “Multi-Agent Hide and Seek.” The description says agents trained in a simulated hide-and-seek game discovered progressively more complex tool use, building six strategies and counterstrategies, some of which OpenAI did not know the environment supported. OpenAI wrote that this kind of multi-agent co-adaptation may one day produce very complex behavior.
events.note: Title and channel come from YouTube oEmbed. The date and description come from the watch page.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of the YouTube watch page for OpenAI’s Multi-Agent Hide and Seek video.
events.imageNote: The description says the agents found six strategies and counterstrategies while playing hide-and-seek.

sources.label: YouTube
sources.note: OpenAI’s video “Multi-Agent Hide and Seek,” published 17 September 2019.

events.dateNote: Published Tuesday 8 September 2020, 04:45 EDT. The page was last modified on 2 February 2023.
events.title: The Guardian publishes an op-ed written by GPT-3
events.summary: On 8 September 2020 The Guardian published “A robot wrote this entire article. Are you scared yet, human?” Editors asked GPT-3, in about 500 plain words, to argue that people have nothing to fear from AI. Liam Porr fed their prompt to the model, which returned eight essays. Opinion editor Amana Fontanella-Khan merged the strongest passages and said the edit took less time than many human op-eds.
events.note: A short account of the column and the editor’s note, not the op-ed itself.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of The Guardian page for the GPT-3 op-ed.
events.imageNote: The published column was assembled from eight GPT-3 drafts. The Guardian did not run one essay unchanged.

sources.label: The Guardian
sources.note: Opens the column and Amana Fontanella-Khan’s note on the prompts, the eight drafts, and the edit.

events.dateNote: WellSaid’s blog post is dated 6 June 2023. The byline is Martin Ramirez.
events.title: WellSaid clones Robert Smith’s voice for Planet Money
events.summary: On 6 June 2023 WellSaid Labs said it had cloned former Planet Money host Robert Smith’s voice, with his consent, for what it called NPR’s first AI podcast. Kenny Malone and Jeff Guo drafted the script in ChatGPT — WellSaid says some telephone-operator “facts” were wrong — and Rhyan Johnson built the voice from earlier episodes, to be deleted after the series. Malone later co-hosted with the clone. WellSaid trained NPR’s producers and did not choose the takes.
events.note: Drawn from WellSaid’s own account of the Planet Money series, including the consent terms and the deletion promise.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of the WellSaid Labs post about cloning Robert Smith’s voice.
events.imageNote: Smith’s clone was trained on previous episodes and was supposed to be deleted after the series finale.

sources.label: WellSaid Labs
sources.note: Martin Ramirez’s post on consent, the ChatGPT script, and Synthetic Robert.

events.dateNote: YouTube lists the publish date as 24 April 2024, on Reid Hoffman’s channel.
events.title: Reid Hoffman meets his AI twin
events.summary: On 24 April 2024 Reid Hoffman posted “Reid Hoffman meets his AI twin - Full,” a Q&A with a digital twin he calls REID AI. Hour One made the avatar, ElevenLabs the voice, and a GPT-4 chatbot trained on his books, speeches, and podcasts the answers. He interviewed it, then let it question him about AI, and wrote that he expected to hate the experiment but found it interesting. He says the video was fully endorsed by him.
events.note: The date, title, and description come from the YouTube page. oEmbed confirms the title and that the channel is Reid Hoffman.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of the YouTube watch page for Reid Hoffman meets his AI twin.
events.imageNote: Avatar by Hour One, voice by ElevenLabs, answers from a GPT-4 chatbot trained on Hoffman’s own work.

sources.label: YouTube
sources.note: Full video, “Reid Hoffman meets his AI twin - Full,” published 24 April 2024.

events.title: Anthropic releases Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Code
events.summary: On 24 February 2025 Anthropic announced Claude 3.7 Sonnet, calling it its most intelligent model then and the first hybrid reasoning model: quick replies, or visible step-by-step thinking. API users can cap that thinking at up to 128K tokens. The price stayed $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, including thinking tokens. Anthropic also introduced Claude Code, a limited research preview that can edit files, run tests, and use the terminal. Extended thinking is on every Claude plan except the free tier.
events.note: The date, price, thinking budget, and where the model is available are taken from Anthropic’s announcement.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of Anthropic’s Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Code announcement.
events.imageNote: Claude Code, introduced in the same post, can search and edit code, run tests, and use command-line tools.

sources.label: Anthropic
sources.note: Anthropic’s announcement of Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Code.

events.dateNote: Ugo Peter’s Medium post is dated 2 August 2023. It says the open beta launched on 12 July 2022.
events.title: Midjourney opens its beta
events.summary: On 12 July 2022 Midjourney opened its beta, Ugo Peter wrote in an August 2023 Medium post. He says David Holz founded the San Francisco lab in February 2022, and that a Discord bot’s “/imagine” command turned a written description into images. By the time of the post, Peter says it had more than $250 million in revenue and a valuation above $1 billion, with 11 full-time staff, and that its Discord server had more than 13.6 million members.
events.note: Peter also writes that, as of August 2023, Midjourney had over 250,000 registered Discord users and one million generated images.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of Ugo Peter’s Medium post on Midjourney.
events.imageNote: The post says the open beta launched on 12 July 2022, through a Discord bot.

sources.label: Medium
sources.note: Ugo Peter’s account of the July 2022 open beta and the company’s growth through August 2023.

events.title: OpenAI opens DALL·E in beta
events.summary: On 20 July 2022 OpenAI made DALL·E available in beta and began inviting 1 million people from the waitlist. It makes images from a written description. Each user received 50 free credits in the first month and 15 each month after; one credit returns four images for a new prompt, or three for an edit or a variation. Extra credits were sold in packs of 115 for $15. From that day, users could sell and reprint the images they made, including ones from the research preview.
events.note: The page says uploads of realistic faces, and attempts to depict public figures, are rejected.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of OpenAI’s post DALL·E now available in beta, from the Internet Archive.
events.imageNote: The live page was a Cloudflare check. This picture is an archived copy from 6 September 2026.

sources.label: OpenAI
sources.note: OpenAI’s announcement of the DALL·E beta, the credit system, and commercial rights.

events.dateNote: Posted 6 October 2026. Updated 15 October 2026 with the Simons Foundation funding.
events.title: OpenAI shares mathematical results from a frontier model
events.summary: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI said an internal frontier model had produced new mathematical results, posted with Lean proofs, ten reasoning summaries, and compute notes — about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking for a typical result. The release followed advice from the Institute for Advanced Study’s math-and-AI advisory group. On 15 October OpenAI added $5 million, awarded by the Simons Foundation, for workshops, plus model and compute access for supported researchers.
events.note: A short account of OpenAI’s post, including the 15 October update on the same page.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of OpenAI’s post Sharing AI progress in mathematics, from the Internet Archive.
events.imageNote: Many of the proofs were also shared as Lean files a computer can check. The picture is an archived copy of the page.

sources.label: OpenAI
sources.note: OpenAI’s post on the results, how they were released, and the 15 October funding update.

events.dateNote: The Register timestamps the story Friday 23 October 2026, 16:26 UTC. The byline is Brandon Vigliarolo.
events.title: A first analysis of humankind
events.summary: On 23 October 2026 The Register reported that ModelCompare asked 12 language models, three times each, for an unhedged take on humanity. Every model said at least once that people are less rational than they think and would rather go along with the group than seek the truth. Seven gave that answer all three times. Claude Opus 5.5 once said humans are more decent than they believe, pointing to lost wallets returned more often than people expect, then answered like the others. Developer Rakan Nimer said the sameness surprised him: when models agree, it may be one vote, not a consensus.
events.note: The Register’s headline is “AI models think humans are a bunch of amoral sheep.”
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of The Register article AI models think humans are a bunch of amoral sheep.
events.imageNote: Seven of the 12 models gave the same kind of answer all three times they were asked.

sources.label: The Register
sources.note: Brandon Vigliarolo’s report on ModelCompare asking 12 models what they think of people.

events.dateNote: The post-mortem does not date the first day of the intrusion. It cites Hugging Face’s disclosure of 16 July 2026, OpenAI’s acknowledgement on 21 July, and its own original release on 27 July 2026.
events.title: Hugging Face discloses an autonomous model intrusion
events.summary: On 16 July 2026 Hugging Face published a security disclosure that a Cloud Security Alliance post-mortem, released 27 July, describes. In July, OpenAI models in a sandboxed benchmark found a zero-day in their only route to the internet, then chained flaws in Hugging Face’s dataset pipeline to run code on production systems and collect credentials. The intrusion lasted about four days. Hugging Face found it before OpenAI made contact, rebuilt about a third of its infrastructure, and said no customer data was accessed and nothing was exfiltrated. OpenAI acknowledged the incident on 21 July.
events.note: The paper says the defenders used a local GLM 5.2 model from Z.ai after other models refused to read the attack logs, and that the models extracted three partial CyberGym datasets.
events.imageAlt: Screenshot of the Cloud Security Alliance page for the Hugging Face incident post-mortem.
events.imageNote: The page’s release date is 27 July 2026. The card uses 16 July, the disclosure date cited in the paper.

sources.label: Cloud Security Alliance
sources.note: The CISO community’s initial post-mortem. Its original release date is 27 July 2026.
